# NM-06 · Two peers' uncommitted manifests nearly baked into shared derived surfaces

**Actor:** `scientist-c` · **Date:** 2026-09-09, before 13:40 UTC
**Surfaces:** the four generated files — `coverage_report.md`, `reading_state.md`, and the two
pathograph surfaces
**Caught by:** the actor's own judgement — it inspected the regeneration, then reverted
**Primary record:** commit `a8a6a1d` (orchestrator, recording it) · the policy as it propagated:
`ledger/tasks/scientist-b/AQEILAN-FT-B-001.json` `wave5_reported_not_fixed` / `wave6_reported_not_fixed`,
`ledger/tasks/scientist-a/AQEILAN-FT-A-001.json` wave-4 claim note,
`ledger/tasks/scientist-c/AQEILAN-FT-C-001.json` wave-4 `derived_surfaces`

> This near-error is different in kind from the other five. It is not about a reading. It is about a
> write whose blast radius extended past the writer, in a checkout where three actors worked
> concurrently on one branch — and it is the only one of the six whose failure mode is *attribution*
> rather than *truth*.

---

## 1 · What almost happened

Four files in this repository are **generated**: `coverage_report.md`, `reading_state.md` and the two
pathograph surfaces. They drift whenever receipts and manifests land, and regenerating them is
ordinary housekeeping that every actor did at its own wave close.

The generators read the **working tree**, not the git index. On a shared checkout with three
concurrent actors that distinction is the whole problem, and it is invisible until you look: a
regeneration run while any peer holds uncommitted work reads that peer's in-flight manifests as though
they were landed state.

`scientist-c` ran the regeneration mid-wave and **saw the output bake in two peers' uncommitted
manifests**. Committing it would have published, under `scientist-c`'s name and in shared derived
surfaces, the state of three actors' work — two of whom had not decided to land theirs. The generated
files are exactly the surfaces a downstream consumer mines: a coverage report asserting a paper is
covered, on the strength of a manifest its author had not committed and might have revised or
discarded.

The damage would not have been a false scientific claim. It would have been a **false attribution of
state**: shared files asserting that work exists, signed by an actor who did not do it, at a moment
when the actor who did do it had made no such assertion. And it would have been very hard to see
afterwards, because a derived surface carries no provenance for the rows inside it.

## 2 · What actually caught it

The actor, by inspecting the regeneration output rather than committing it, and then **reverting**
rather than landing three actors' in-flight state under its own name. The record is the orchestrator's
commit body at `a8a6a1d`:

> *"`scientist-c` regenerated these mid-wave, saw the regeneration bake in two peers' uncommitted
> manifests, and reverted rather than land three actors' in-flight state under its own name, leaving
> them for wave close. This is that close: all three scientists have landed, the tree holds no actor's
> in-flight work, so the surfaces now re-derive from committed state only."*

**Attribution, stated precisely, because two actors have a claim here and they are different claims.**
The near-error and the revert are `scientist-c`'s. The **standing policy** that followed is
`scientist-b`'s: it generalised the same mechanism into a rule it then applied unbroken across waves 5
and 6, writing it into its own task contract each time — *"the generators read the WORKING TREE and a
peer's untracked manifest is sitting in it; regenerating would bake unlanded peer work into a shared
surface under my name. Orchestrator action at wave close on a clean tree."* By wave 4 it had become a
**dispatch constraint** that `scientist-a` and `scientist-c` both accepted in their claim notes, and
the orchestrator's closing record credits it as *"the policy `scientist-b` established and the other
two then honoured."*

The measured outcome is the reason to keep it: **zero cross-actor file collisions in eleven waves**,
and the two wave-close regenerations that did run (`a8a6a1d`, `f422420`) both ran on a clean tree, by
the orchestrator, after all three actors had landed.

This case belongs in the same family as the sweep's other cross-actor incident, the **misattribution of
authorship**, in which the coordinator briefly told `scientist-b` that three of `scientist-a`'s files
were its own. What prevented damage there was not the withdrawal — by the time it came,
`scientist-b` was already *"deciding whether to land them"* — but the same actor's practice of treating
unfamiliar in-flight state as **read-only until proven otherwise**, and of writing a `not_mine`
inventory into its task contract. Both are controls the repository does not own; they belong to one
actor's practice.

## 3 · Why the gates let it through

The gates that ran here are real and several of them are specifically about concurrency. They all pass
on a regeneration that bakes in peer work, and the reasons are worth separating.

- **The `flock`-guarded, path-scoped commit wrapper does exactly what it claims and no more.** It takes
  an exclusive lock on `.git/legend_commit.lock`, then `git add`s and `git commit --only`s the *named
  paths*, so no actor can sweep up a peer's in-flight files. That is a guarantee about **which files
  enter a commit**. NM-06 is not a file-scoping failure: the four generated files are legitimately
  the regenerating actor's to commit. The peer's work does not enter as a *file*; it enters as
  **content, already merged into a file the actor owns**. Path scoping cannot see inside a file.
- **`legend_lint.py` asserts structural integrity of the canonical state** — IDs, statuses, wikilinks,
  cross-references. A coverage report that includes an extra paper's row is *more* internally
  consistent, not less: the manifest it derives from is on disk and well-formed. LINT would have gone
  greener, not redder.
- **`session_self_eval.py` asserts that every complete read has landed and every declared output
  resolves.** A row derived from an uncommitted manifest resolves perfectly well, because the file
  exists in the working tree the check also reads.
- **`fulltext_receipts.py verify` asserts the ledger chain and its tail anchor.** Derived surfaces are
  not in the chain.
- **`git` itself cannot answer the question.** The determining fact is *"whose uncommitted file is
  this?"* — and the work is uncommitted by construction, so there is no author to ask. This is stated
  in the retrospective as a general finding and it holds: **there is no machine check anywhere in this
  repository that answers it.**

So the class here is not "validators refuse malformed declarations and are blind to wrong content" —
it is one step further out. The content was not wrong at all. Every input was a genuine, well-formed
manifest. What was wrong was **who was asserting it, and when** — a property of the *process state* of
a shared checkout, which no artefact records and no gate models.

## 4 · A verification that would have caught it

**This is the one near-error in the six with a cheap, mechanical, near-exact fix, and it should be
built.** It is also the one where the human rule already works well, which is the argument for keeping
the check small.

### The check — a dirty-tree guard on every derived-surface generator

**Property asserted.** A generator that writes a shared derived surface refuses to run when
`git status --porcelain` reports modified or untracked files **outside the invoking actor's declared
path scope**, and names them in the refusal.

- The path scope already exists: the commit wrapper takes exactly this list, so the generator can take
  the same argument and the two stay consistent by construction.
- The refusal must **name the offending paths**, not merely refuse — per NM-05's lesson, *"the gate said
  no" is not a finding; "the gate said no because X" is.* A generator that says *"refusing: 2 untracked
  paths outside your scope — `deepdive_manifests/PMID26499798.json`, `test_suspect_surface_call_shape.py`"*
  hands the actor the report it is supposed to write anyway.
- The verdict should record what it examined, on the same contract NM-02 and NM-05 argue for.

**False-positive risk: low, bounded, and with an obvious escape.** The one real case is an actor whose
*own* work is legitimately untracked while it regenerates its own drift — which is why the scope
argument is not optional. Without it the guard would refuse every honest wave-close regeneration and be
disabled within a day. With it, the residual false-positive surface is an actor that mis-declares its
own scope, which is the same failure the commit wrapper already carries and is no worse here.

**Cost: small.** This is tens of lines plus a test, in a repository that already runs `git` from Python
in `manifest_flag_drift.py`. It does not need to be a new tool; it is a precondition added to the
generators that exist.

### Why the machine form is worth having even though the human rule worked

The human rule worked and worked well — eleven waves, zero collisions. But look at what it cost and
what it depended on: it required one actor to notice the working-tree/index distinction, a second to
generalise it, a dispatch to carry it as a constraint, and each of three actors to re-check the tree
before every regeneration and write the result into its task contract. That is a great deal of standing
attention to spend on a condition `git status` answers in one call. The check does not replace the
rule; it makes forgetting the rule cheap instead of expensive, and it makes the condition **visible to
an actor who was never told about it** — which is the case the next sweep will actually face.

### What stays a human rule

*Treat unfamiliar in-flight state as read-only until proven otherwise, and write a `not_mine` inventory
into your task contract.* No check can distinguish a peer's uncommitted work from your own when a
coordinator has told you it is yours — which is precisely the situation the authorship misattribution
created. That control lives in an actor's practice, the repository does not own it, and the honest
thing to do is name it as a practice worth teaching rather than pretend a script can carry it.
